turns.output: Every Sunday afternoon, my grandmother's kitchen filled with the savory perfume of vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, and bay leaves simmering together. That was how we knew chicken adobo was coming, and that the whole family would soon gather around her wooden table, hungry and happy. This recipe is hers, carried from Batangas to California in a notebook stained with decades of splatters and love. Adobo is often called the unofficial national dish of the Philippines, but in our home it was Lola's chicken: tender, glossy, salty, sour, and just a little sweet. She taught us that patience matters, that chicken should brown before it braises, and that no one leaves the table without rice for the sauce. I have made it for birthdays, heartbreaks, and Tuesdays. Now I am sharing it with you, hoping it brings your family the same comfort, conversation, and second helpings it has always brought mine.

Every family has one dish that brings everyone to the table without a single call, and for ours, it is chicken adobo. The moment garlic hits hot oil and vinegar begins to simmer with soy sauce, black peppercorns, and bay leaves, the whole house smells like home. My grandmother made it every Sunday, tasting the sauce with a spoon and adjusting it by memory alone. My mother learned by standing beside her, watching, stirring, and listening to stories that never made it into any cookbook. Now I make it for my own children, who argue over the last piece of chicken and spoon extra sauce over warm rice. This recipe is simple, forgiving, and deeply comforting, built on balance rather than strict rules. It is salty, tangy, savory, and just a little sweet. Make it once, taste as you go, and soon it will become part of your family story.

Imagine sunlight isn't just white — it's actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow traveling together.

When that sunlight reaches Earth, it has to pass through our atmosphere, a blanket of air made of teeny-tiny molecules, much smaller than you can see. As the light bumps into these molecules, it gets scattered — bounced around in all directions. This is called Rayleigh scattering.

Here's the trick: different colors behave differently. Blue light has short, choppy waves, so it gets knocked around easily and scatters everywhere. Red, orange, and yellow light have longer, smoother waves, so they mostly sail straight through with less bouncing.

So during the day, blue light is scattered all over the sky above you. Whichever direction you look, some of that scattered blue light reaches your eyes, making the whole sky look blue.

At sunset, it's different. The sunlight has to travel through much more air to reach you, so most of the blue gets scattered away before it arrives. That leaves the reds and oranges behind — which is why sunsets look so fiery and beautiful!

Pretty cool, right? The sky isn't painted blue — it's light playing a bouncing game overhead!

Have you ever wondered why the sky looks blue instead of green or purple?

Sunlight looks white, but it is actually made of many colors mixed together, like a rainbow. You can see those colors when light passes through a prism or when a rainbow appears after rain.

When sunlight reaches Earth, it travels through the air around our planet. That air is full of tiny particles and gas molecules that are much smaller than you can see. As the light hits them, it bounces and scatters in different directions.

Here is the important part. Blue light has short, choppy waves, so it gets scattered much more easily than other colors. Red and orange light have longer waves, so they mostly travel straight through with less scattering.

Because blue light is scattered all over the sky, it reaches your eyes from every direction. Wherever you look up, you see that scattered blue light, so the whole sky appears blue.

At sunset, sunlight has to travel through more air to reach you. Most of the blue light gets scattered away before it arrives, leaving reds and oranges for you to enjoy.

When you visit a website, your browser has to download lots of files from the internet: text, images, logos, and code that tells the page how to look and behave. Downloading all of that takes time and data.

A browser cache is like a storage box on your computer where the browser keeps copies of some of those files after your first visit.

Next time you visit the same site, the browser checks its cache first. If it already has a recent copy of the logo, background image, or other files, it loads them instantly from your computer instead of downloading them again. This makes pages load much faster and uses less internet data.

Not everything is stored forever. Websites tell the browser how long to keep each file. Some files might be kept for a few hours, others for weeks. When a file expires, or the website updates it, the browser downloads a fresh copy and replaces the old one.

Sometimes the cache can cause problems, like showing an old version of a page. That's why you might hear advice to "clear your cache" — it empties the storage box, forcing the browser to download everything fresh.

When you visit a website, your browser has to download many files, such as images, logos, styles, and scripts. Downloading them takes time and uses data, especially on a slow connection.

A browser cache solves this problem by saving copies of some of those files on your own computer. Think of it like keeping a snack in your desk drawer instead of walking to a store every time you feel hungry.

The first time you visit a page, the browser downloads the files and stores them in the cache. The website can also tell the browser how long each file should be kept.

When you return to the same page later, the browser first checks its cache. If it finds a fresh copy of a file, it uses that copy right away instead of downloading it again. This makes the page load much faster and reduces the amount of data you use.

If a file is too old, missing, or has changed on the website, the browser downloads a new version and updates the cache.

Sometimes the cache can show an outdated page. Clearing the cache forces the browser to download everything fresh again.

One year ago, I traded code reviews for career conversations — and learned more than I expected.

Here are 5 lessons from my first year as an engineering manager:

1. Your job is no longer to have the best solution. It's to create space for your team to find it.

2. 1:1s aren't status updates. They're where trust is built, blockers surface early, and people feel heard.

3. Context is kindness. Engineers don't resist decisions they understand — they resist decisions they don't.

4. Feedback delayed is feedback denied. Small, timely, and specific beats perfect and late.

5. You can't pour from an empty cup. Protecting my focus time made me a better manager, not a less available one.

I still miss building. But watching engineers grow, ship, and surprise themselves? That's the new build that matters.

To new managers: What surprised you most?

#EngineeringLeadership #Management

One year ago, I became an engineering manager. I thought the job was about having better technical answers. I was wrong.

Here are five lessons I learned:

1. Listening beats solving. My team rarely needed my solution first. They needed to feel heard, then space to think.

2. One on ones are the real work. Trust is built in small, consistent conversations, not big announcements.

3. Clear is kind. Vague feedback helped no one. Specific, timely, respectful feedback helped people grow.

4. Protect focus. My calendar became a team tool. Fewer meetings and clearer priorities gave engineers time to do deep work.

5. Let go of code. My value now comes from unblocking others, asking good questions, and creating clarity.

I still miss building things directly. But helping others build, grow, and succeed is even more rewarding.

Grateful for a team that taught me more than I taught them.

To new managers: What surprised you most?

#EngineeringManagement #Leadership

Jane Austen's *Pride and Prejudice* (1813) follows Elizabeth Bennet, the sharp-witted second of five daughters in a modest English family under pressure to marry well. When the wealthy Mr. Bingley rents a nearby estate, he falls for Elizabeth's sister Jane, while his proud friend Mr. Darcy clashes with Elizabeth. Misjudging Darcy as arrogant and believing false tales from the charming Wickham, Elizabeth rejects Darcy's first proposal. Darcy, meanwhile, must confront his own pride and class prejudice. Through letters, scandals — including Lydia Bennet's elopement — and Darcy's secret intervention to save the family's reputation, Elizabeth learns she misjudged him. Both change: Darcy becomes humbler and more generous, Elizabeth more self-aware. They eventually marry for love and mutual respect, as do Jane and Bingley.

Its themes include pride and prejudice as barriers to understanding, the rigid class hierarchy and economic necessity of marriage for women, reputation and propriety, and the tension between first impressions and true character. Austen satirizes a society that values wealth and status over integrity, while celebrating intelligence, moral growth, and marriages based on equality rather than convenience or passion alone. Ultimately, the novel suggests true love requires self-knowledge, humility, and willingness to see beyond social expectations and snap judgments.

Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice follows Elizabeth Bennet, the sharp and independent second daughter of a modest English family with five daughters and no son to inherit their estate. When the wealthy Mr. Bingley rents a nearby home, he falls for Elizabeth's gentle sister Jane, while his proud friend Mr. Darcy offends Elizabeth with his arrogance. Misjudgments multiply through gossip, family embarrassment, and the manipulations of the charming but dishonest Mr. Wickham. Elizabeth rejects Darcy's first proposal, angered by his interference in Jane's romance and his treatment of Wickham. Later, she learns the truth about Wickham's character and sees Darcy's quiet generosity, especially when he helps rescue her youngest sister from scandal. Both characters confront their flaws, Elizabeth her prejudice and Darcy his pride, and they eventually marry for love and respect.

The novel explores class, money, and marriage in a society where women depend on husbands for security. Austen satirizes snobbery and foolishness while valuing intelligence, integrity, and self knowledge. She shows that first impressions can mislead and that real worth lies beneath social rank. Through Elizabeth's growth, Austen argues that love should rest on understanding and character rather than wealth or appearance alone.

1/5 Clever code feels brilliant when you write it. Simple code feels brilliant when you have to read, debug, and change it six months later.

You’ll spend 10x more time reading code than writing it — optimize for the reader.

2/5 Clever code shows how smart the author is. Simple code shows how much the author cares about the next person.

That next person is usually future you, tired, under pressure, and fixing a production bug.

3/5 Every clever trick adds hidden costs: more edge cases, harder onboarding, and code nobody wants to touch.

Simple code is boring and predictable — and in software, boring is reliable.

4/5 As Brian Kernighan said: “Debugging is twice as hard as writing code. If you write the cleverest code you can, you are, by definition, not smart enough to debug it.”

5/5 The goal isn’t the shortest one-liner. It’s code so obvious a new teammate can understand it in minutes.

Write for humans first, computers second. Simple wins.

1/5 Clever code feels great to write. Simple code feels great to read, debug, and change six months later. Guess which one your team does more often.

2/5 Simple code is easier to review. When logic is obvious, reviewers can spot real bugs instead of spending all their energy just trying to understand what the code does.

3/5 Simple code fails in simple ways. When something breaks at 2 a.m., you want clear logic you can follow step by step, not a puzzle that only its author can solve.

4/5 Simple code is easier to extend. New teammates can add features, fix edge cases, and refactor with confidence because they do not have to decode hidden tricks first.

5/5 Cleverness has a cost, and everyone after you pays it. Write the boring version. Your future self, your teammates, and your users will thank you.

Well, we did grow up, but thankfully, we never grew apart. I've watched Maya face every challenge with kindness, humor, and that stubborn determination we all love. I wondered if anyone could ever match her heart.

Then she met Daniel. I saw her laugh louder, dream bigger, and become even more herself. Daniel, you don't just love Maya for who she is; you celebrate her for it. That's rare, and that's real.

Maya, I'm so proud of the woman you've become, and so grateful I get to stand beside you today, just like I did on the playground all those years ago.
